Hi Doctor NerdLove,
I need advice about a situation and hope you can help me with it.

I am autistic and have difficulties with getting along with people. I have a small number of close friends, most of them I know for a very long time. They are about the amount of social contact I can manage.

Since I did not think that dating or a relationship would ever work for me, I started visiting brothels when I first had enough money to afford it. This is legal and regulated here in Germany. I have continued doing this until today, with an average of around six visits per month.

Normally I see the same woman for some time, until another woman catches my interest. Sometimes I also book more than one woman. I have a well-paid government job and no particularly expensive hobbies or other large expenses, so the money is not a problem for me.

I also have a close female friend whom I know since kindergarten. We talk about almost everything, including our sex lives. She always seemed to be very interested when I told her about my experiences in the brothel. Sometimes we even discussed which woman I should book next, and she helped me to make a decision. Afterwards, she also often wanted to know how it was.

Recently she got out of an abusive relationship, and I helped her as much as I could. At the moment she is in France for a longer business trip. We were talking online about some other things when I mentioned that I had been feeling very horny lately and was looking forward to my next appointment.

She then told me that she had been feeling lonely and that, if I wanted, we could also have sex with each other. She was quite clear she was not looking for a relationship, dating and that she had no intention of catching feelings. Just sex between friends, without further expectations.

I was very surprised by this suggestion, because I had never considered her as a possible sexual partner before. I told her that I was very honored by the offer and tempted by it. I said that I thought it was an idea worth trying when she returns. Since then, we have been texting each other in a more flirtatious manner than usual.

I have been thinking about this situation quite a lot. The fact is that I would very much like to have sex with her. But I am concerned that I could damage our friendship, because I have no experience with sexual encounters where the other person is not being paid.

With the women from the brothels, I have always tried to behave respectfully. I ask them which things they do not want to do and if they tell me to stop something, I stop immediately. I also give them a tip in person in addition to paying the bill at the brothel, but I must also be honest that their enjoyment was not really the priority in those encounters.

However, I understand that sex with my friend would be a different situation. I would also want to make sure that she enjoys the experience. I know that she said there should be no feelings or further expectations involved. I have no reason to assume that she is lying about this. But I also know that people sometimes have feelings or reactions they did not expect beforehand. I am not sure how much I should be concerned about this possibility, or if I am making the situation more complicated than it needs to be.

There is also the question of what I should actually do. So I would appreciate some practical advice about how to handle this. Should we discuss everything in detail before we have sex? How do I find out what she wants me to do without making the whole situation unnecessarily formal? And is there anything specific I should do afterwards to make sure that our friendship can continue as it was before?

I care about this friendship a lot, and I do not want to lose it because I handled one situation badly. I also do not want to reject an opportunity that could be enjoyable for both of us simply because I do not understand all the social rules involved.
Thank you in advance for your advice.
Germanic Loner

The self-induced stress of trying to repress, ignore or manage those feelings tend to cause far more damage to the friendship than the feelings themselves, especially if the person feeling them is responding to discussions in their head, rather than with their friend.

What I would recommend is that instead of saying “hey, no feelings” would be for the two of you to resolve that you’re going to keep open communication and be willing to talk if things do come up for one or both of you. Like every human being, I have preferences and boundaries when it comes to dating. Some of mine are quite specific.
For example, if I meet a woman, get to know her over a period, and she eventually develops an interest in me only after dating or sleeping with other men, I’d choose to never date her.

I’m writing this letter because I have found myself in that situation (again). I met a woman just over a year ago, and we got along very well from the beginning. We have always had a good laugh, and I’ve enjoyed getting to know her. That said, our interactions have taken place almost exclusively at the class we attend, with a little bit of texting, and there has never been any romantic or sexual tension between us. About three months ago, she went on holiday. When she came back, she naturally told me a little about her trip, including that she had met a local guy while she was away, and had a fling with him. I didn’t think anything of it. As far as I was concerned, she was simply sharing an interesting story about her holiday with someone she felt comfortable talking to.

However, she recently asked me out for coffee. I was perfectly happy to meet up, but I wanted to establish what she had in mind, so I asked whether she meant it as a date. She said she was open to seeing how things developed. I immediately told her that I would be happy to meet for coffee, but only as friends.
This isn’t the first time I’ve experienced something similar.

I was once friends with a woman for around six years. Not long after we first met, she entered a relationship, which lasted about four years. After they broke up, she took some time for herself. As far as I know, she subsequently had a couple of hookups before deciding that she wanted a relationship again.

It wasn’t long after this that she told me that she had developed feelings for me and asked whether I wanted to spend time together romantically. I said no. Unfortunately, she couldn’t accept my answer, and the situation ultimately brought the friendship to an end.

It’s a pattern that has repeated itself. I’ve got to know someone over a period, only for them to express an interest much later, always after they’ve been in long-term relationships (that started when we knew each other), or when they have had a period of casual encounters.

I absolutely refuse to be someone’s backup option, or second choice. I don’t see how I can see myself as valued or truly desired if the person had to wait X number of years before finally deciding I was worth a chance, meanwhile another guy walks into their life and they are dating / sleeping together within a month. I know I’m not a man that will ever ignite passion in a woman from day one, but likewise I’m not going to allow myself be a guy that someone finally decides is okay enough”.

I have never been involved with a woman, and I’m conscious that I’m reaching an age where my dating options may become more limited even without having boundaries like this. Ultimately, I don’t expect anyone to owe me attraction, nor do I believe that someone is wrong for developing feelings for me later in life. What I want is to feel genuinely chosen and appreciated by the person I’m with. I just don’t see how that’s possible within the contexts that I’m presenting here.

So, am I being unreasonable in needing that feeling of being chosen from the outset, or is this a reasonable boundary to have, even if it significantly narrows my dating pool? And perhaps more importantly, is there a meaningful difference between protecting yourself from being someone’s second choice and simply refusing to accept that people’s feelings can change over time?
Second Choice Is First Loser

here’s the thing about boundaries, SCFL: “reasonable” doesn’t really come into it. What’s “reasonable” to one person is over the top to another, and “absolutely fucking mandatory” for a third, and they’re all correct. You are free to set your boundaries where you choose, for whatever reason. Other people can have opinions, but they don’t get a vote.
https://www.doctornerdlove.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/shutterstock_1721152858.jpg

Now if you want my opinion… I think you’re cutting off your nose to spite your face. While I understand that what you’re wanting is to protect yourself emotionally, I think you’re doing so in a way that’s ultimately counterproductive for what you actually want and it’s getting in the way of relationships that you would find meaningful and fulfilling.

The thing is, I understand what you’re getting at. Everyone wants to feel chosen for their own sake; nobody likes feeling like they’re the backup choice. “You’ll do” are decidedly not the sexiest words in the English language. But I think you’re working from a misapprehension of how attraction and interest work and how people date.

To use an inelegant metaphor, think about what you have for lunch. If you usually get burgers at lunch but after a while you decide you’d rather have tacos instead, does that mean that tacos were your “backup choice”? Does the fact that you had burgers before mean you like tacos less? Or do those decisions exist entirely separate of one another, without judgement about which is “better” or “worse?” Similarly, the kind of food you may order for a meal may just reflect where you are at that moment; maybe you’re feeling like having a lighter option, or you just want something quick and satisfying, even if it’s not the same “quality” as a more elaborate meal.

Sometimes it’s about convenience or what’s easily available to you. Sometimes it’s about the type of experience you want. Other times, it’s about what you’re able to handle. And still other times, it can be about being interested in something new or different or that you’ve been thinking of but haven’t quite been at the point of ordering. But in all of those cases, it’s not about one thing being inherently better than another or something being a backup choice. You can have a hamburger without saying it’s better or worse than steak.

To drag this kicking and screaming back to your question: people choose who they date and sleep with based on a lot of factors. People will, for example have sex not because they’re necessarily attracted to the other person but because they want validation or to prove a point. They may want to sleep with someone because what they want is an uncomplicated experience that’s strictly about getting a particular itch scratched, but not want a relationship. Or they may have gotten out of a relationship and want to reassure themselves that they’re not hung up on that other person. Hell, sometimes it really is as simple as “I’m horny and/or lonely and this person is the least objectionable option that presented themselves at the moment.”

That doesn’t say anything about the person they slept with previously, nor about the person they may sleep with later; it’s about that particular point in time. That’s not even remotely the same as “well, option A wasn’t available, let’s move to option B”, especially if they’re interested in a potentially committed relationship.
(Yes, you can find individuals who will do this because people are incredibly diverse. It’s almost always very obvious and they’re absurdly easy to see coming a mile away.)

In all of the cases you mention and the ones you infer, none of them are people who are looking at you as the “second choice”. Those relationships and hook ups had nothing to do with you, and while they don’t exist in a complete vacuum (because no decision we make does) that doesn’t mean that you’re the backup plan when they didn’t work. In each of them it seems pretty clear that these are people who were interested in you because you’re you and were making overtures in good faith. The fact that they had relationships and/or hook ups before doesn’t say anything about how they feel about you. Even the fact that they may have started a relationship after they met you doesn’t mean that they were rejecting you or not “giving you a chance”.

Honestly, even the fact that you’re describing this as “giving you a chance” is part of what’s screwing you up here. You’re treating this as though this is something you were entitled to but denied, and that they’re insulting you by coming to you later. Just changing that phrasing and outlook is going to change how you see these relationships; you’re looking at them from a place of aggrievement, not connection, and I’m betting there’s even a certain amount of spite involved in rejecting them. That’s a really unhealthy way to look at this, and it’s going to get in the way of being able to actually have a happy and mutually fulfilling relationship.

Here’s something I think you need to understand: people develop feelings for others at their own pace. Ignore all the redpill-manosphere bullshit that says “women know in 5 seconds if they’ll ever be attracted to you” and listen to women who will talk about how they became attracted to someone that they hadn’t been before. The fact that you may have been interested in them from the start doesn’t mean that they were interested in you. You may not have pinged their radar at the time, but you do now for all sorts of reasons.

What they don’t do is develop feelings at the exact same time as other people, or right when they meet. Shit, Dr. Mrs. The NerdLove and I were friends for over a decade before she and I even thought about the possibility of dating, never mind doing anything about it. As we have both said: if it were going to happen sooner, it would have. We both had to become the people we grew into in order to be right for one another.

People are incredibly complex and often contradictory. What we are not – no matter how much we try to convince ourselves otherwise – are purely rational actors, and expecting people to behave that way is a mistake. We will deny ourselves things that we know we want because we feel like we can’t or “shouldn’t” have them, for reasons that make no rational sense but make sense to us in that moment. We will pursue things that we may not actually want or recognize at some level are bad for us for a whole host of reasons, from social expectations to attachment styles, from a lack of confidence to simply feeling like it’s something we should want.

We grow, we change, what we want or need or find appealing or desirable change with us, all the time. What made sense to us at one phase in our lives will seem absolutely absurd at another. That’s part of how growth works. This is particularly true when it involves people we know; the more we spend time with someone and the better we get to know them, the more we come to appreciate their uniqueness that makes them special. This also affects how we see them – as individuals and as potential partners.

Do you know why someone might, after knowing you for years, decide that they want to date you? It’s in part because they’ve known you for years. Their understanding of you and of themselves has often changed as they’ve lived their lives. They may have grown an appreciation for you, as we grow an appreciation for things that are strongly flavored. Or they may have seen changes in you that weren’t there when you first met. Or they may have thought that they couldn’t be in a relationship with you for any number of reasons, even if they wanted one. And none of these reasons have anything to do with “you’re the second-tier option”. That’s just self-limiting fuckery and the sort of misery that grievance-peddling slapdicks want you to wallow in so they can sell you bullshit solutions.

Like I said: I understand the impulse behind this belief and boundary. It’s a form of self-protection. But like many other examples, this is a form of self-protection that has long outlasted its usefulness and instead has become a form of self-limitation and harm mixed with a wounded pride. A wound that, to be perfectly blunt, is almost entirely self-inflicted and that you refuse to let heal.

You can set boundaries where you choose, at any time and for any reason. But just because you chose to set it doesn’t mean you should keep it, especially if it neither serves its intended purpose, nor prevents you from harm.

You want my opinion? It’s time to let go of this one, to recognize how much this belief has been holding you back for no reason and to let go of that sense of indignant spite towards people who are just trying to connect with you.
I’m willing to bet you’ll be a hell of a lot happier if you do.
Good luck.

Just… wow.” can help make it clear that this was a good experience for you, not something you regret.

If there’s a surge of emotions, that’s entirely ok. Be open to them, be willing to listen if either of you need to say something or express them. Those post-coital moments afterwards can feel vulnerable; be as non-judgmental and accepting as you can. You may have done something that you haven’t done together before, but that doesn’t mean that you have to be stiff or weird with her. You’ve got this, GL. Write back and let us know how it goes.

Good luck.

Like every human being, I have preferences and boundaries when it comes to dating. Some of mine are quite specific.

For example, if I meet a woman, get to know her over a period, and she eventually develops an interest in me only after dating or sleeping with other men, I’d choose to never date her.

I’m writing this letter because I have found myself in that situation (again). I met a woman just over a year ago, and we got along very well from the beginning. We have always had a good laugh, and I’ve enjoyed getting to know her. That said, our interactions have taken place almost exclusively at the class we attend, with a little bit of texting, and there has never been any romantic or sexual tension between us. About three months ago, she went on holiday. When she came back, she naturally told me a little about her trip, including that she had met a local guy while she was away, and had a fling with him. I didn’t think anything of it. As far as I was concerned, she was simply sharing an interesting story about her holiday with someone she felt comfortable talking to.

However, she recently asked me out for coffee. I was perfectly happy to meet up, but I wanted to establish what she had in mind, so I asked whether she meant it as a date. She said she was open to seeing how things developed. I immediately told her that I would be happy to meet for coffee, but only as friends.

This isn’t the first time I’ve experienced something similar.

I was once friends with a woman for around six years. Not long after we first met, she entered a relationship, which lasted about four years. After they broke up, she took some time for herself. As far as I know, she subsequently had a couple of hookups before deciding that she wanted a relationship again.

It wasn’t long after this that she told me that she had developed feelings for me and asked whether I wanted to spend time together romantically. I said no. Unfortunately, she couldn’t accept my answer, and the situation ultimately brought the friendship to an end.

It’s a pattern that has repeated itself. I’ve got to know someone over a period, only for them to express an interest much later, always after they’ve been in long-term relationships (that started when we knew each other), or when they have had a period of casual encounters.

I absolutely refuse to be someone’s backup option, or second choice. I don’t see how I can see myself as valued or truly desired if the person had to wait X number of years before finally deciding I was worth a chance, meanwhile another guy walks into their life and they are dating / sleeping together within a month. I know I’m not a man that will ever ignite passion in a woman from day one, but likewise I’m not going to allow myself be a guy that someone finally decides is okay enough”.

I have never been involved with a woman, and I’m conscious that I’m reaching an age where my dating options may become more limited even without having boundaries like this. Ultimately, I don’t expect anyone to owe me attraction, nor do I believe that someone is wrong for developing feelings for me later in life. What I want is to feel genuinely chosen and appreciated by the person I’m with. I just don’t see how that’s possible within the contexts that I’m presenting here.

So, am I being unreasonable in needing that feeling of being chosen from the outset, or is this a reasonable boundary to have, even if it significantly narrows my dating pool? And perhaps more importantly, is there a meaningful difference between protecting yourself from being someone’s second choice and simply refusing to accept that people’s feelings can change over time?

Second Choice Is First Loser

here’s the thing about boundaries, SCFL: “reasonable” doesn’t really come into it. What’s “reasonable” to one person is over the top to another, and “absolutely fucking mandatory” for a third, and they’re all correct. You are free to set your boundaries where you choose, for whatever reason. Other people can have opinions, but they don’t get a vote.

Now if you want my opinion… I think you’re cutting off your nose to spite your face. While I understand that what you’re wanting is to protect yourself emotionally, I think you’re doing so in a way that’s ultimately counterproductive for what you actually want and it’s getting in the way of relationships that you would find meaningful and fulfilling.

The thing is, I understand what you’re getting at. Everyone wants to feel chosen for their own sake; nobody likes feeling like they’re the backup choice. “You’ll do” are decidedly not the sexiest words in the English language. But I think you’re working from a misapprehension of how attraction and interest work and how people date.

To use an inelegant metaphor, think about what you have for lunch. If you usually get burgers at lunch but after a while you decide you’d rather have tacos instead, does that mean that tacos were your “backup choice”? Does the fact that you had burgers before mean you like tacos less? Or do those decisions exist entirely separate of one another, without judgement about which is “better” or “worse?” Similarly, the kind of food you may order for a meal may just reflect where you are at that moment; maybe you’re feeling like having a lighter option, or you just want something quick and satisfying, even if it’s not the same “quality” as a more elaborate meal.

Sometimes it’s about convenience or what’s easily available to you. Sometimes it’s about the type of experience you want. Other times, it’s about what you’re able to handle. And still other times, it can be about being interested in something new or different or that you’ve been thinking of but haven’t quite been at the point of ordering. But in all of those cases, it’s not about one thing being inherently better than another or something being a backup choice. You can have a hamburger without saying it’s better or worse than steak.

To drag this kicking and screaming back to your question: people choose who they date and sleep with based on a lot of factors. People will, for example have sex not because they’re necessarily attracted to the other person but because they want validation or to prove a point. They may want to sleep with someone because what they want is an uncomplicated experience that’s strictly about getting a particular itch scratched, but not want a relationship. Or they may have gotten out of a relationship and want to reassure themselves that they’re not hung up on that other person. Hell, sometimes it really is as simple as “I’m horny and/or lonely and this person is the least objectionable option that presented themselves at the moment.”

That doesn’t say anything about the person they slept with previously, nor about the person they may sleep with later; it’s about that particular point in time. That’s not even remotely the same as “well, option A wasn’t available, let’s move to option B”, especially if they’re interested in a potentially committed relationship.

(Yes, you can find individuals who will do this because people are incredibly diverse. It’s almost always very obvious and they’re absurdly easy to see coming a mile away.)

In all of the cases you mention and the ones you infer, none of them are people who are looking at you as the “second choice”. Those relationships and hook ups had nothing to do with you, and while they don’t exist in a complete vacuum (because no decision we make does) that doesn’t mean that you’re the backup plan when they didn’t work. In each of them it seems pretty clear that these are people who were interested in you because you’re you and were making overtures in good faith. The fact that they had relationships and/or hook ups before doesn’t say anything about how they feel about you. Even the fact that they may have started a relationship after they met you doesn’t mean that they were rejecting you or not “giving you a chance”.

Honestly, even the fact that you’re describing this as “giving you a chance” is part of what’s screwing you up here. You’re treating this as though this is something you were entitled to but denied, and that they’re insulting you by coming to you later. Just changing that phrasing and outlook is going to change how you see these relationships; you’re looking at them from a place of aggrievement, not connection, and I’m betting there’s even a certain amount of spite involved in rejecting them. That’s a really unhealthy way to look at this, and it’s going to get in the way of being able to actually have a happy and mutually fulfilling relationship.

Here’s something I think you need to understand: people develop feelings for others at their own pace. Ignore all the redpill-manosphere bullshit that says “women know in 5 seconds if they’ll ever be attracted to you” and listen to women who will talk about how they became attracted to someone that they hadn’t been before. The fact that you may have been interested in them from the start doesn’t mean that they were interested in you. You may not have pinged their radar at the time, but you do now for all sorts of reasons.

What they don’t do is develop feelings at the exact same time as other people, or right when they meet. Shit, Dr. Mrs. The NerdLove and I were friends for over a decade before she and I even thought about the possibility of dating, never mind doing anything about it. As we have both said: if it were going to happen sooner, it would have. We both had to become the people we grew into in order to be right for one another.

People are incredibly complex and often contradictory. What we are not – no matter how much we try to convince ourselves otherwise – are purely rational actors, and expecting people to behave that way is a mistake. We will deny ourselves things that we know we want because we feel like we can’t or “shouldn’t” have them, for reasons that make no rational sense but make sense to us in that moment. We will pursue things that we may not actually want or recognize at some level are bad for us for a whole host of reasons, from social expectations to attachment styles, from a lack of confidence to simply feeling like it’s something we should want.

We grow, we change, what we want or need or find appealing or desirable change with us, all the time. What made sense to us at one phase in our lives will seem absolutely absurd at another. That’s part of how growth works. This is particularly true when it involves people we know; the more we spend time with someone and the better we get to know them, the more we come to appreciate their uniqueness that makes them special. This also affects how we see them – as individuals and as potential partners.

Do you know why someone might, after knowing you for years, decide that they want to date you? It’s in part because they’ve known you for years. Their understanding of you and of themselves has often changed as they’ve lived their lives. They may have grown an appreciation for you, as we grow an appreciation for things that are strongly flavored. Or they may have seen changes in you that weren’t there when you first met. Or they may have thought that they couldn’t be in a relationship with you for any number of reasons, even if they wanted one. And none of these reasons have anything to do with “you’re the second-tier option”. That’s just self-limiting fuckery and the sort of misery that grievance-peddling slapdicks want you to wallow in so they can sell you bullshit solutions.

Like I said: I understand the impulse behind this belief and boundary. It’s a form of self-protection. But like many other examples, this is a form of self-protection that has long outlasted its usefulness and instead has become a form of self-limitation and harm mixed with a wounded pride. A wound that, to be perfectly blunt, is almost entirely self-inflicted and that you refuse to let heal.

You can set boundaries where you choose, at any time and for any reason. But just because you chose to set it doesn’t mean you should keep it, especially if it neither serves its intended purpose, nor prevents you from harm.

You want my opinion? It’s time to let go of this one, to recognize how much this belief has been holding you back for no reason and to let go of that sense of indignant spite towards people who are just trying to connect with you.

I’m willing to bet you’ll be a hell of a lot happier if you do.

Good luck.
